newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - OPEC agrees a new 6-month quota freeze.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - OPEC agrees a new 6-month quota freeze.

text.p: OPEC oil ministers agreed at Vienna talks on Wednesday to freeze their current production quotas until the end of the year in an attempt to boost world oil prices.
Crude oil futures jumped on the news with the benchmark North Sea Brent Blend for August delivery advancing more than 40 cents to $18.30 per barrel before it eased slightly.
The quota accord that is being extended sets a ceiling on total volume by the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries at 25.03 million barrels daily.
Chronic violations have, in fact, lifted actual output some two million above that.
Announcing Wednesday's decision, however, OPEC secretary-general Rilwanu Lukman said that all 11 cartel members gave individual pledges that they would now adhere to mandatory limits.
Lukman said no threats had been made against alleged violators - they are led by Venezuela - but that they had made promises to colleagues and OPEC believed them.
Some independent analysts who were present in the OPEC lobbies were sceptical.
"People will not believe that anything has changed until they see it," said Leo Drollas, economist at the London-based Centre for Global Energy Studies.
John Lichtblau, head of Petroleum Industry Research Associates, deemed it "unthinkable" that big, cash-pinched violators like Venezuela and Nigeria would cut to quota.
The excess oil had during this year depressed prices to around $18 now from $25 at the end of 1996, particularly angering Iran.

Venezuela's minister was earlier on Wednesday summoned to a private session with Saudi Arabia's Ali Naimi and Gholamrezah Aghazadeh of Iran - which a Gulf delegate said was intended to "emphasise the need for quota compliance".
That sounded like OPEC parlance for a tongue lashing. But beyond that, OPEC has no mechanism to compel a sovereign state to honour its quotas.
Delegates said that Saudi Arabia was in no mood to threaten to turn up the taps on its huge spare capacity as a retaliatory measure.
The new OPEC accord is due to be rubber-stamped at a plenary session of the OPEC conference on Thursday.
